content:
Environmental Assessment of Wood UtilizationAssessing the environmental performance of wood products across their life cycle.
Overview#Wood utilization can contribute to climate change mitigation through carbon storage, material substitution, and the sustainable use of forest resources.
However, its environmental performance depends on multiple stages, including forest management, harvesting, transportation, processing, use, reuse, and disposal.
This project evaluates the environmental impacts and potential benefits of wood utilization using life cycle approaches.
Objectives#Quantify greenhouse gas emissions associated with wood products Evaluate carbon storage throughout product life cycles Compare wood-based products with alternative materials Identify opportunities to reduce environmental impacts Support environmentally responsible wood utilization Research Activities#The project examines environmental impacts across the wood supply chain.
Research activities include:
Collection of forestry and wood-processing data Life cycle inventory development Greenhouse gas accounting Carbon balance assessment Comparison of alternative production and utilization scenarios Evaluation of recycling, reuse, and end-of-life options Methods#The project uses methods such as:
Life Cycle Assessment Carbon footprint analysis Greenhouse gas accounting Scenario analysis Material flow analysis Statistical analysis Expected Outcomes#This research aims to provide quantitative information that supports:
Low-carbon wood production Sustainable material selection Improved forest and wood-product management Regional climate strategies Evidence-based environmental decision-making Related Research Theme#This project is connected to:

content:
Forest ValueEvaluating the environmental, ecological, and social value of forests.
Overview#Forests provide many forms of value beyond timber production.
They support biodiversity, store carbon, regulate water, protect landscapes, and contribute to human well-being. Our laboratory evaluates these values from ecological, environmental, economic, and social perspectives.
Research Questions#How can the multiple values of forests be measured and visualized? How do forest conditions influence ecosystem services? How can forest value be reflected in management and policy decisions? How do people perceive and use forest? Research Topics#Ecosystem services Biodiversity assessment Carbon sequestration Landscape evaluation Sustainable forest management Social and cultural value of forests Methods#We combine field surveys, spatial analysis, environmental assessment, and social surveys to evaluate forest value from multiple perspectives.

Regional Economic Impacts of Local TimberEvaluating how forest resources contribute to regional industries and economic circulation.
Overview#Forestry and wood utilization generate economic activity through forest management, harvesting, transportation, processing, construction, energy use, and related services.
The economic effects of these activities extend beyond the forestry sector itself.
This project evaluates how the production and use of local timber contribute to employment, income, industrial activity, and regional economic circulation.
Objectives#Quantify the economic effects of forestry and wood utilization Evaluate the regional circulation of income and expenditure Identify industries connected to forest-resource use Compare local and non-local timber utilization scenarios Support regional forest and industrial policies Research Activities#The project investigates the relationship between forest resources and regional economies.
Research activities include:
Analysis of forestry and wood-industry production Estimation of direct and indirect economic effects Evaluation of employment and income generation Comparison of timber procurement scenarios Assessment of local supply chains Examination of links between environmental and economic outcomes Methods#The project uses methods such as:
Input–output analysis Regional economic analysis Supply-chain analysis Scenario analysis Statistical data analysis Interviews and field surveys Expected Outcomes#This research aims to support:
Regional forestry strategies Local timber procurement Development of forest-related industries Employment and income creation Sustainable regional resource use Coordination between environmental and economic policies Related Research Theme#This project is connected to:

content:
People, Biodiversity, and SatoyamaExploring relationships between forest ecosystems, local communities, and human activities.
Overview#Satoyama forests have been shaped through long-term interactions between people and forest ecosystems.
Changes in forest use, management practices, population, and local economies can influence biodiversity, resource availability, and community relationships with forests.
This project examines the ecological and social dimensions of satoyama management.
Objectives#Understand relationships between people and satoyama forests Evaluate the effects of forest management on biodiversity Examine local knowledge and forest-resource use Identify factors supporting continued community participation Contribute to sustainable satoyama management Research Activities#The project combines ecological investigation with social and community-based research.
Research activities include:
Forest and biodiversity surveys Investigation of fungal and other biological communities Interviews with residents and forest users Documentation of local forest knowledge Analysis of management practices Evaluation of community participation Methods#The project uses methods such as:
Field surveys Biodiversity assessment Ecological monitoring Interviews and questionnaires Participatory research Qualitative and quantitative analysis Expected Outcomes#This research aims to contribute to:
Sustainable satoyama management Biodiversity conservation Maintenance of local forest knowledge Community-based forest activities Improved understanding of human–forest relationships Integration of ecological and social perspectives Related Research Theme#This project is connected to:

Regional EconomyEvaluating the regional economic impacts of forestry and wood-based industries.
Overview#Forestry and wood utilization generate economic activity through harvesting, transportation, processing, construction, and related local industries.
Our laboratory studies how forest resources and wood-based industries contribute to regional employment, income, production, and economic circulation.
Research Questions#How much economic activity is generated by forestry and wood utilization? Which industries benefit from increased local timber use? How does local procurement affect the regional economy? How can forest-related industries contribute to regional revitalization? Research Topics#Regional economic ripple effects Forestry and timber industries Local procurement Employment and income generation Supply chains Regional revitalization Methods#We use input-output analysis, economic ripple-effect analysis, supply-chain analysis, statistical data, and interviews with local stakeholders.

content:
Satoyama & CommunitiesExploring relationships between forests, biodiversity, culture, and local communities.
Overview#Satoyama landscapes have been shaped through long-term interactions between people and nature.
Changes in population, lifestyles, and forest use have weakened many of these relationships. Our laboratory studies ways to reconnect people with forests through biodiversity, local knowledge, forest products, cultural practices, and community activities.
Research Questions#How have relationships between people and satoyama changed? How can local communities participate in forest management? What ecological and cultural values are maintained through human activity? How can forest products and local traditions support renewed engagement with forests? Research Topics#Satoyama management Community participation Biodiversity and fungal communities Matsutake and forest environments Local knowledge and culture Environmental education Methods#We combine field surveys, fungal and DNA analysis, questionnaires, interviews, participatory observation, and collaborative research with local communities.

This page describes how to transcribe an MP3 meeting recording with OpenAI Whisper on Windows and organize the transcription into meeting minutes with ChatGPT.
FFmpeg is required because Whisper uses it internally to read audio files. The MP3 file does not need to be converted or divided manually.
Workflow#MP3 meeting recording ↓ Whisper reads the MP3 using FFmpeg ↓ Text transcription ↓ ChatGPT organizes the transcription ↓ Manual review and correctionRequirements#Windows Python 3 FFmpeg OpenAI Whisper ChatGPT Install FFmpeg#Whisper requires the FFmpeg command-line tool to read MP3 and other audio files.
Using Chocolatey:
choco install ffmpegAlternatively, using Scoop:
scoop install ffmpegAfter installation, close and reopen PowerShell. Confirm that FFmpeg is available:
ffmpeg -versionIn this workflow, FFmpeg is not used directly to convert or divide the MP3 file. Whisper calls FFmpeg internally when loading the recording.
Install OpenAI Whisper#Install Whisper using pip:
py -m pip install -U openai-whisperConfirm that the whisper command is available:
whisper --helpMove to the Recording Folder#Open PowerShell and move to the folder containing the MP3 recording.
For example:
cd "C:\Users\username\Documents\meeting"Replace the path with the actual location of the recording.
Transcribe the MP3 File#Run Whisper with the MP3 file as its input:
whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format txt --fp16 FalseThe options have the following meanings:
--language Japanese: specifies that the recording is in Japanese --model medium: uses the medium-sized Whisper model --output_format txt: creates a plain-text transcription --fp16 False: uses FP32, which is suitable when processing with a CPU The MP3 file does not need to be converted to WAV beforehand.
After processing, a text file is created in the same folder:
meeting.txtThe first time a model is used, Whisper downloads the corresponding model data. Processing time depends on the length of the recording and the performance of the computer.
Use a Smaller Model#If transcription with the medium model is too slow, use the small model:
whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model small --output_format txt --fp16 FalseA smaller model generally runs faster, although transcription accuracy may differ.
The turbo model can also be used:
whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model turbo --output_format txt --fp16 FalseCreate Additional Output Formats#To create subtitle files and other output formats in addition to the plain-text file, use:
whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format all --fp16 FalseDepending on the installed Whisper version, files such as the following may be generated:
meeting.txt meeting.srt meeting.vtt meeting.tsv meeting.jsonFor creating meeting minutes, the TXT file is usually sufficient.
Create Meeting Minutes with ChatGPT#Upload meeting.txt to ChatGPT and enter a prompt such as the following:
The attached file is an automatic transcription of a meeting conducted in Japanese. Correct obvious transcription errors, repetitions, and false starts, and prepare meeting minutes using the following structure: - Meeting title - Date and time - Participants - Agenda - Decisions - Main discussion points - Unresolved issues - Action items - Person responsible - Deadline - Items to confirm before the next meeting Do not add facts that are not present in the transcription. Mark uncertain names, organization names, technical terms, dates, and numerical values as "要確認". Clearly distinguish between confirmed decisions and ideas that were only discussed.Providing the following information together with the transcription can improve the result:
Participant names Organization names Project names Product names Technical terms Known agenda items For example:
Participants: - Tanaka - Sato - Suzuki Terms that may appear in the recording: - ABC Project - XYZ System - OpenLCAJapanese Prompt Example#The following Japanese prompt can also be used:
添付ファイルは、日本語で行われた会議の自動文字起こしです。 明らかな誤認識、言い直し、重複表現を修正し、次の構成で 議事録を作成してください。 - 会議名 - 日時 - 参加者 - 議題 - 決定事項 - 議論の要点 - 未決事項 - アクション項目 - 担当者 - 期限 - 次回までの確認事項 文字起こしに含まれていない事実は追加しないでください。 判断できない人名、組織名、専門用語、日付、数値には 「要確認」と記載してください。 正式に決定された事項と、単に案として議論された事項を 明確に区別してください。Troubleshooting#The ffmpeg Command Is Not Found#If the following command fails:
ffmpeg -versionclose and reopen PowerShell after installing FFmpeg.
If it still fails, confirm that FFmpeg has been added to the Windows PATH environment variable.
The whisper Command Is Not Found#Try running Whisper through Python:
py -m whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format txt --fp16 FalseAlso confirm the installation:
py -m pip show openai-whisperPowerShell Cannot Find the MP3 File#Confirm the current folder:
Get-LocationList the files in the folder:
Get-ChildItemAlternatively, specify the full path to the MP3 file:
whisper "C:\Users\username\Documents\meeting\meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format txt --fp16 FalseThe File Name Contains Spaces#Place the file name or path inside quotation marks:
whisper "meeting recording.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format txt --fp16 FalseNotes#Automatic transcription may incorrectly recognize:
Personal names Organization names Technical terms Abbreviations Dates Numerical values Statements made by overlapping speakers The generated meeting minutes should therefore be checked against the original recording.
Before recording or processing a meeting, confirm participant consent and the applicable rules regarding confidential information, personal information, and the use of external AI services.
For confidential meetings, consider removing sensitive information before uploading the transcription to ChatGPT.
Summary#The actual transcription command is simple:
whisper "meeting.mp3" --language Japanese --model medium --output_format txt --fp16 FalseAlthough FFmpeg is not called directly in this workflow, it must be installed because Whisper uses it internally to read the MP3 recording.

content:
This page provides a Python script for creating a timelapse video from a sequence of image files.
Requirements#Python OpenCV tqdm Install the required libraries with:
pip install opencv-python tqdmDownload#Download timelapse.py →
Python Script#import cv2 import os import glob # パラメータ設定 image_folder = "images" # 画像フォルダのパス output_video = "timelapse.mp4" # 出力動画ファイル名 frame_rate = 30 # フレームレート（例：30fps） # 画像ファイル一覧を取得（連番ファイルを想定） image_files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(image_folder, "*.jpg"))) if not image_files: raise ValueError("指定フォルダに画像がありません。") # 最初の画像から解像度を取得 first_image = cv2.imread(image_files[0]) height, width, layers = first_image.shape resolution = (width, height) # 動画ライターの設定 fourcc = cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'mp4v') # MP4用コーデック video_writer = cv2.VideoWriter( output_video, fourcc, frame_rate, resolution ) # 画像を順に動画に追加 for img_file in image_files: img = cv2.imread(img_file) if img is None: print(f"警告: {img_file} を読み込めません。スキップします。") continue img_resized = cv2.resize(img, resolution) video_writer.write(img_resized) video_writer.release() print(f"タイムラプス動画を作成しました: {output_video}")Usage#Save the script as timelapse.py.
Place the image files in the specified folder and run:
python timelapse.pyNotes#Image files should be arranged in chronological order. All images should preferably have the same dimensions. The frame rate and output resolution can be changed in the script. Related Media#View the Megumi Forest Timelapse →

content:
The Forest Environmental Assessment Laboratory studies how forests and wood create value for people, regions, and the environment.Our work is based on the idea that forests should not be evaluated only as ecosystems or natural resources. Forests also create environmental, economic, social, and cultural value.We aim to make these values visible and to explore how they can support sustainable forest use, regional economies, and renewed relationships between people and forests.Our MissionOur mission is to evaluate the value of forests and wood from multiple perspectives.
We study:
the environmental performance of wood and forest utilization;the economic impacts of forestry and wood use on local and regional economies;the social and cultural values that connect people with satoyama forests;the conditions needed to return forests to regional cycles of everyday life and resource use.Integrating Natural and Social SciencesMany forest-related issues cannot be understood through natural science or social science alone.For example, the ecological value of a satoyama forest may depend on soil conditions, fungi, vegetation, and biodiversity. At the same time, whether local residents return to the forest may depend on economic incentives, cultural meaning, local knowledge, and social relationships.For this reason, our laboratory combines methods from both fields.Our research includes environmental assessment, economic analysis, forest and soil surveys, DNA and fungal analysis, GIS, interviews, questionnaire surveys, and collaborative research with local communities.Creating Value from ForestsWood can have environmental advantages over materials such as concrete and steel.Locally produced wood may also generate employment, income, and economic activity within a region.Satoyama forests may regain meaning through resources such as mushrooms, biodiversity, landscape value, local knowledge, and opportunities for community participation.We investigate how these different forms of value can be measured, communicated, and used to create more sustainable relationships between forests and society.CollaborationWe welcome collaboration with:
students and researchers;local residents and community groups;forestry and wood-related businesses;public organizations and local governments;schools and educational institutions;anyone interested in forests, wood utilization, and regional sustainability.Learn about our research →
View our projects →
Access and contact →

content:
Research Philosophy#Forests provide far more than timber. They generate environmental, economic, social, and cultural value that supports sustainable communities.
Our laboratory studies how these values can be measured, visualized, and utilized to reconnect forests with people’s everyday lives.
Research Themes#🌲 Forest ValueEvaluating ecosystem services, biodiversity,landscape functions, and the environmental value of forests.🪵 Wood UtilizationLife Cycle Assessment (LCA), carbon storage,greenhouse gas accounting, and sustainable use of wood.📈 Regional EconomyRegional economic impacts of forestry,wood industries, and sustainable regional development.🤝 Satoyama & CommunitiesConnecting forests and people throughsatoyama management, biodiversity,and local community activities.Research Methods#Our research integrates methods from both natural and social sciences.
🌲 Forest ecology and field surveys 🪵 Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) 🌍 Greenhouse gas accounting 📈 Input–output and regional economic analysis 🛰 GIS and spatial analysis 🍄 Fungal and DNA analysis 📝 Questionnaire and interview surveys 🤝 Collaborative research with local communities Current Projects#Current research topics include:
Environmental performance of wood utilization Carbon storage and climate benefits of wood products Regional economic impacts of forestry and timber industries Sustainable management of satoyama landscapes Biodiversity and fungal communities Community participation in forest management Continue Exploring#📂ProjectsExplore our ongoing and completed research projects.Explore Projects →📚PublicationsView journal articles, reports, and other research outputs.View Publications →👥MembersMeet the researchers and students in our laboratory.Meet the Team →
